opening_complaint: Both hands are stiff and swollen when I wake up.
hpi_onset: Eight weeks of bilateral hand symptoms.
hpi_location: The knuckles where my fingers meet my hands and the middle finger joints, on both sides.
hpi_quality: Achy, puffy and hard to bend.
hpi_severity: It is about 5 out of 10. Opening jars and fastening buttons are difficult.
hpi_timing: At least an hour, sometimes an hour and a half.
hpi_chronology: It started in a few fingers and now affects both hands most days.
Progressed from several fingers to bilateral daily symptoms.
hpi_setting: I had a mild cold just before it began. A child at the daycare had a slapped-cheek rash.
A mild cold preceded the joint symptoms. A child at the daycare had a slapped-cheek rash.
hpi_aggravating: Sitting still for a long time makes me stiff again.
hpi_alleviating: A warm shower and gently moving them.
hpi_treatment: Ibuprofen 200 milligrams twice on a few days helped somewhat, but it upset my stomach.
Partial relief but dyspepsia with intermittent ibuprofen 200 mg twice daily.
history_medical_history: I have hypothyroidism, treated for 6 years.
history_surgery: My gallbladder was removed 4 years ago.
history_medicines: Levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning, and the occasional ibuprofen I mentioned.
history_drug_reactions: Amoxicillin caused hives as an adult, without breathing trouble.
history_work: I work at a daycare, lifting children and opening food containers.
Daycare worker; hand function affects lifting and containers.
history_support: My partner helps with our toddler, but missing work for appointments is difficult.
Partner helps with toddler; appointment-related work absence is difficult.
history_family_history: My mother has rheumatoid arthritis. My father has arthritis in his finger tips.

history_sibling: One brother, with no major illness that I know of.

model_note.S:
CC: Both hands are stiff and swollen when I wake up.

HPI: 38-year-old female. Eight weeks of bilateral hand symptoms. Bilateral MCP and PIP symptoms. Aching, swelling and stiffness. 5/10; difficulty with jars and buttons. Morning stiffness 60–90 minutes. Progressed from several fingers to bilateral daily symptoms. A mild cold preceded the joint symptoms. A child at the daycare had a slapped-cheek rash. Stiffness after inactivity. Relief with warmth and movement. Partial relief but dyspepsia with intermittent ibuprofen 200 mg twice daily. No similar previous episode.

PMH: Hypothyroidism for 6 years.

PSH: Cholecystectomy 4 years ago.

Meds: Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily; intermittent ibuprofen.

SH: Never smoked. No alcohol. No recreational drugs. Daycare worker; hand function affects lifting and containers. Partner helps with toddler; appointment-related work absence is difficult. LMP 1 week ago; condoms; pregnancy test not obtained.

FH: Mother: rheumatoid arthritis; father: distal finger arthritis. Brother: no known major illness.

Allergies: Amoxicillin: hives without respiratory symptoms.

ROS: Musculoskeletal: Symmetric finger-joint swelling. Associated wrist arthralgia. No myalgia. General: Fatigue. No fever. No weight loss. Skin: No rash or psoriasis-like plaques. No photosensitive rash. No nail changes.
model_note.O:
Vitals: BP 114/70 mmHg, P 80 bpm, R 16 rpm, T 98.6 F oral, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 5", Wt 148 lbs

General: Alert, mildly tired appearing.
Musculoskeletal: Symmetric swelling of second and third MCP and PIP joints; no DIP swelling or deformity. Boggy tenderness of affected MCP/PIP joints and mild bilateral wrist tenderness. Finger flexion limited by pain and swelling; wrist flexion mildly painful bilaterally. Grip strength mildly reduced bilaterally by pain; proximal arm strength 5/5.
Skin: No rash on inspected arms or palms; no nail pitting.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: Clear bilateral breath sounds.
Osteopathic: T1 bilateral paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
P: 1. Arrange urgent rheumatology referral for persistent small-joint synovitis; do not wait for laboratory results. Obtain RF, anti-CCP, CBC, renal/liver profile and ESR/CRP, with hand/foot imaging as appropriate. Discuss early disease-modifying treatment assessment, joint protection and safe symptom relief; review within 1–2 weeks to confirm access. A hot single joint or fever needs urgent evaluation.

2. Assess whether parvovirus testing would clarify the exposure and prolonged course; avoid attributing persistent synovitis to a past cold alone. Offer supportive analgesia and explain pregnancy/exposure discussion if relevant.

3. If degenerative disease remains after inflammatory assessment, consider radiographs and occupational therapy for hand function, pacing and adaptive aids. Explain that symptomatic measures do not replace evaluation of synovitis.
